title: Drivers of bat activity at wind turbines advocate for mitigating bat exposure using multicriteria algorithm-based curtailment
abstract: Wind turbine development is growing exponentially and faster than other sources of renewable energy worldwide. While multi-turbine facilities have small physical footprint, they are not free from negative impacts on wildlife. This is particularly true for bats, whose population viability can be threatened by wind turbines through mortality events due to collisions. Wind turbine curtailment (hereafter referred to as “blanket curtailment”) in non-winter periods at low wind speeds and mild temperatures (i.e. when bats are active and wind energy production is low) can reduce fatalities, but show variable and incomplete effectiveness because other factors affect fatality risks including landscape features, rain, turbine functioning, and seasonality. The combined effects of these drivers, and their potential as criteria in algorithm-based curtailment, have so far received little attention. We compiled bat acoustic data recorded over four years at 34 wind turbine nacelles in France from post-construction regulatory studies, including 8619 entire nights (251 ± 58 nights per wind turbine on average). We modelled nightly bat activity in relation to its multiple drivers for three bat guilds, and assessed whether curtailment based on algorithm would be more efficient to limit bat exposure than blanket curtailment based on various combinations of unique wind speed and temperature thresholds. We found that landscape features, weather conditions, seasonality, and turbine functioning determine bat activity at nacelles. Algorithm-based curtailment is more efficient than blanket curtailment, and has the potential to drastically reduce bat exposure while sustaining the same energy production. Compared to blanket curtailment, the algorithm curtailment reduces average exposure by 20 to 29 % and 7 to 12 % for the high-risk guilds of long- and mid-range echolocators, and by 24 to 31 % for the low-risk guild of short-range echolocators. These findings call for the use of algorithm curtailment as both power production and biodiversity benefits will be higher in most situations.

## 49 **1. Introduction**

- 50 Wind power generation produces near-zero greenhouse gas emissions during the operational

- 51 phase, has short greenhouse gas payback time, and constitutes an efficient and sustainable

- 52 way for the transition towards reduced global greenhouse gas emissions (Dammeier et al.,

- 53 2019; Veers et al., 2019). As a consequence and in line with international treaties such as the

- 54 2016 Paris agreement to reduce global greenhouse gas emissions, wind turbine installation has

- 55 grown exponentially over the last 20 years and currently represents the most rapidly

- 56 expanding form of renewable energy worldwide (GWEC, 2021). While wind farm installation

- 57 can have a relatively small footprint in terms of land conversion compared to other 58 development projects, it still entails negative impacts on wildlife, particularly for

- 59 insectivorous bats through mortality events by collision. Such increases in mortality are likely

- 60 to impinge on the viability of populations (Friedenberg and Frick, 2021; Frick et al., 2017).

- 61 This is especially true for migratory and long-range echolocating bat species, which are the

- 62 most sensitive to collisions as they fly more often at the height at which turbines operate

- 63 (Roemer et al., 2017). In addition to mortality, some bat species avoid areas adjacent to wind 64 turbines leading to a reduction of habitat availability (Barré et al., 2018).

- 65 In the European Union and in many countries worldwide, wind energy developers must carry

- 66 out an Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA) prior to any wind farm installation to

- 67 evaluate potential environmental consequences and the measures required to avoid impacts.

- 68 Developers must also monitor impacts during the operational phase (e.g. decree no. 0198 of

- 69 August 27, 2011, in France). However, guidelines to avoid “areas where high bat activity has

- 70 been determined by impact assessment” (EUROBATS; Rodrigues et al., 2015) appear to be

- 71 poorly implemented (Barré et al., 2022). When impacts cannot be avoided, measures fot their

- 72 reduction or, as a last resort, offsetting, must be implemented to achieve a state of no net loss

- 73 of biodiversity (i.e. the mitigation hierarchy framework; Business and Biodiversity Offsets

- 74 Programme (BBOP), 2012). Wind turbine curtailment at low wind speeds and mild

- 75 temperatures – when bats are highly active and energy production is low, hereafter referred to

- 76 as “blanket curtailment” – is a reduction measure that offers promising opportunities to

- 77 reconcile bat conservation and wind energy (Adams et al., 2021; Whitby et al., 2021; Voigt et

- 78 al., 2015; Arnett et al., 2011; Baerwald et al., 2009). One of the most common blanket

- 79 curtailment strategies is based on a simple combination of a maximum wind speed threshold

- 80 (most often between 3.5 and 8 m/s) and a minimum temperature threshold (most often around

- 81 10°C). Respectively below and above those thresholds, the blades are turned to a different

- 82 angle (i.e. feathered) to limit their rotation rate to less than one per minute, due to expected 83 favourable conditions for bats. Blanket curtailment is mostly limited to non-winter periods.

- 84 This approach can significantly reduce the fatality risk, but shows variable and incomplete 85 effectiveness (Voigt et al., 2022; Adams et al., 2021; Whitby et al., 2021; Măntoiu et al.,

- 86 2020). Besides wind speed and temperature, landscape features and other weather factors such

- 87 as rain also drive bat fatality risk (Thompson et al., 2017; Santos et al., 2013). Indeed, bat

- 88 activity at wind turbine nacelles, which links to fatality risk ( Peterson et al., 2021; Korner-

- 89 Nievergelt et al., 2013), also depends on the weather, season, landscape features, and wind

- 90 turbine dimensions and rotation speed (Roemer et al., 2019; Behr et al., 2017; Cryan et al.,

- 91 2014; Brinkmann et al., 2011; Horn et al., 2008). Consequently, curtailment strategies based

- 92 on multifactor algorithms have the potential to be more efficient in reducing the fatality risk.

- 93 Indeed, the use of an algorithm to curtail wind turbines in real-time based on weather factors,

- 94 date, and nightly time, should allow avoiding most collisions while minimizing the loss of 95 production (Behr et al., 2017).

- 96 Behr et al. (2017) and Brinkmann et al. (2011) are two of the few studies that propose this

- 97 type of multicriteria framework to curtail wind turbines. These studies were based on data

- 98 sampled in 2008 in Germany covering six months at 70 wind turbine nacelles and 35 different

- 99 sites. To our knowledge, no peer-reviewed study has examined simultaneously and on a

- 100 spatiotemporally extensive dataset all drivers of bat exposure (i.e. landscape features, weather

- 101 conditions, date, and wind turbine characteristics), nor assessed the possibility to use them in

- 102 guild specific algorithms to inform wind turbine curtailment.

- 103 To assess the potential of multicriteria curtailment algorithms, we compiled bat acoustic data

- 104 recorded at wind turbine nacelles in France by wind energy developers in a context of post-

- 105 construction regulatory studies, while homogeneously re-analysing acoustic data (i.e. using

- 106 the same automated bat call identification software). Reprocessed bat acoustic data allowed us

- 107 to build a standardised bat activity metric at nacelle height known to be a good predictor of

- 108 fatality risk (Peterson et al., 2021; Korner-Nievergelt et al., 2013). Given the absence of

- 109 national guidelines in France concerning the characteristics and settings of bat recorders for

- 110 bat monitoring at nacelles and the large number of engineering consultants involved in data

- 111 collection, we expected a large variation in the methods (Coly et al., 2017). Thus, our first

- 112 objective was to assess whether monitoring methods (devices and settings) or confounding

- 113 effects with landscape features, date, weather and wind turbine characteristics would bias the

- 114 comparison of bat activity between wind turbines. This assessment was intended to filter out 115 data from some wind turbines if necessary, and highlight the need for better national or

- 116 international cooperation in the choice of materials and parameters in the case where the

- 117 current situation would not allow meta-analyses. Once any method bias was controlled for,

- 118 our second objective was to determine the main factors influencing bat activity at nacelles.

- 119 We expected bat activity to increase with increasing landscape quality (e.g. by an increasing

- 120 amount of forests, proximity to wetlands, or land use heterogeneity; Put et al., 2019; Sirami et

- 121 al., 2013; Boughey et al., 2011a) and decreasing blade rotation speed (Cryan et al., 2014;

- 122 Horn et al., 2008), and to be higher during nights with good weather conditions (i.e. high

- 123 temperature, low wind speed and no rain; Voigt et al., 2015; Erickson and West, 2002) and at

- 124 the end of summer (Heim et al., 2016). Finally, our third objective was to compare on a per-

- 125 night scale the performance of a curtailment algorithm based on multiple factors to that of a

- 126 blanket curtailment method based on various combinations of unique wind speed and

- 127 temperature thresholds, in terms of both bat activity exposure and energy production. We

- 128 expected the algorithm-based curtailment to be more efficient in reducing bat exposure

- 129 compared to blanket curtailment, by avoiding a larger percentage of bat activity occurring

- 130 when blades are moving, while involving smaller losses of energy production.

## 131 **2. Methods**

- 132 _2.1. Acoustic data collection and processing_

- 133 We compiled existing raw acoustic data (i.e. sound files in raw or wav format) of 14,937

- 134 complete recording nights at 59 wind turbine nacelles (including 20 models) located on 55

- 135 wind farms in France (Fig. 1; Table S1). These data were provided by nine wind farm

- 136 developers and produced by 12 consulting firms and non-governmental organizations as part

- 137 of regulatory post-implementation impact monitoring studies. Each of the 59 wind turbines

- 138 was monitored on average for 251 nights (min: 103; max: 514). The monitored nights covered

- 139 all months of the year and spanned four years between 2017 and 2020; 10% of the sites were

- 140 monitored for more than one year. The year 2017 represents 2% of nights, 2018 18% of

- 141 nights, 2019 79% of nights and 2020 0.4% of nights (Fig. S1). Depending on the analyses 142 conducted, the complete set or subset of these data were used (see Statistical analysis section).

- 143 Three types of recorders were used: Batcorder at 18 wind turbines (versions 1, 2 and 3; 144 ecoObs), Batmode S+ at 34 wind turbines (bat bioacoustics technology GmbH), and Song

- 145 Meters at eight wind turbines (SM3BAT and SM4BAT; Wildlife Acoustics). All recorders

- 146 were positioned at the bottom of the nacelle. Each was associated with one to three triggering

- 147 thresholds, i.e. a built-in recording control algorithm which started the recording when a

- 148 sound event exceeded a given sound level (see Supporting information S1 for more details).

- 149 Acoustic monitoring was always performed throughout the night, from sunset to sunrise. We

- 150 used the number of bat passes (hereafter referred to as “activity”) or the presence/absence

- 151 (hereafter referred to as “occurrence”) recorded during a night as a measure of bat visits with

- 152 exposure (see section 2.3 for more details). We defined a bat pass as one or more echolocation

- 153 calls within a five-second interval (Kerbiriou et al., 2019). All 731,717 bat passes were

- 154 automatically classified to the closest taxonomic level using the Tadarida software (Bas et al.,

- 155 2017). Since most bat species had very low occurrence (Table S1), we pooled together species

- 156 into three guilds based on their similar echolocation call structures and therefore similar

- 157 foraging strategies: long-range echolocators (LRE), mid-range echolocators (MRE) and short-

- 158 range echolocators (SRE) (Frey-Ehrenbold et al., 2013), see Table S2 for species

- 159 composition. Long-range echolocators are especially sensitive to fatality risks with wind

- 160 turbines due to the great part of the time they spend at height (i.e. 20 to 45 m above ground

- 161 level), followed by the mid-range echolocators (Table S2; Roemer et al., 2017). Although

- 162 grouping species into these three guilds prevented misidentification problems between cryptic

- 163 species, noise in the nacelle due to wind turbine functioning generated many false positives,

- 164 especially at very high blade speeds. We followed the approach of Barré et al. (2019) and 165 applied a maximum false positive tolerance of 50% to discard these interferences (see Barré et 166 al. (2019) for more details), which reduced the dataset to 98,627 bat passes. This reduction led 167 to discard 6.55 to 9.93% fewer false positives for Batmode data compared to other recorders.

- 168

- 169 _2.2. Environmental and wind turbine variables_

- 170 To determine which factors influence bat activity and occurrence at wind turbine nacelles, we

- 171 collected or computed variables related to landscape composition and heterogeneity, weather 172 conditions, and wind turbine functioning and dimensions.

- 173 _Landscape variables_ - We considered variables representing the surface cover of five land-use

- 174 types  known to positively or negatively affect bats: impervious surfaces (Azam et al., 2016;

- 175 Dixon, 2011), arable lands (Put et al., 2019), grasslands (Froidevaux et al., 2017; Roeleke et

- 176 al., 2016; Lentini et al., 2012), forests (Heim et al., 2017; Boughey et al., 2011a) and water

- 177 bodies (De Conno et al., 2018; Sirami et al., 2013). These variables were computed around

- 178 the 59 wind turbines as proportions of the total area for variables presenting enough variations

- 179 (impervious surfaces, arable lands, grasslands and forests), in ten area buffers around wind

- 180 turbines (50, 100, 250, 500, 1000, 2000, 3000, 4000, 5000 and 10000 m radius) to use the

- 181 most relevant scale for each variable (Kalda et al., 2015, see Statistical Analysis section for

- 182 more details). We also calculated the Euclidean distance to the nearest impervious surfaces,

- 183 forests and water bodies. Moreover, we computed landscape metrics depicting landscape

- 184 configurational and compositional heterogeneity (Monck-Whipp et al., 2017), including edge

- 185 density (i.e. the density of ecotones in m/ha), conditional entropy (i.e. an increasing index

- 186 with increasing landscape complexity), patch richness density (i.e. the number of patch types

- 187 standardised by the surface), and Shannon diversity index of habitat patches. These landscape

- 188 metrics were computed using the R package _landscapemetrics_ (Hesselbarth et al., 2019), for 189 the ten radius sizes presented above. All landscape variables were extracted from the high190 resolution CES OSO land cover map 2018 available at https://www.theia-

- 191 land.fr/en/ceslist/land-cover-sec/  (Derksen et al., 2020).

- 192 _Weather variables_ - We collected the average wind speed (m/s) and temperature (°C) 193 recorded by wind turbine nacelle weather stations in 10-minute intervals and averaged them 194 on a nightly scale at each wind turbine (i.e. on the same scale as acoustic data). Since the

- 195 amount of rainfall was not recorded by the nacelle weather stations, we collected the daily

- 196 cumulated rain (mm) (i.e. over the 24-hour period from midnight of the day when the 197 recording night started) using the weather database from E-OBS 198 (https://surfobs.climate.copernicus.eu/dataaccess/access_eobs.php#datafiles).

- 199 _Wind turbines variables_ - We collected dimensions of wind turbines which measured 45 to

- 200 139 m (92 m on average) in nacelle height and 44 to 126 m (94 m on average) in rotor

- 201 diameter (Table S1). We also collected the average rotation speed (km/h) at the tip of the

- 202 blade in 10-minute intervals, and averaged it on a nightly scale at each wind turbine.

- 203

- 204 _2.3. Statistical analysis_

- 205 We assessed drivers of measures of bat activity and occurrence around wind turbine nacelles,

- 206 including factors related to landscape composition and heterogeneity, weather conditions, the

- 207 Julian day, wind turbine functioning and dimensions and recording methods (i.e. the recorder

- 208 type and the trigger sensitivity). In the first step, since we compiled data produced by different

- 209 contributors, we expected the existence of multiple combinations between the recorder type

- 210 and the trigger sensitivity. However, these recording methods deeply affect the number of bat 211 passes recorded (Adams et al., 2012). Confounding effects between recording methods and

- 212 factors of interest (e.g. landscape composition) could prevent modeling them simultaneously.

- 213 Using all compiled data, we therefore tested for trends in the landscape composition and 214 heterogeneity, weather conditions, and wind turbine functioning and dimensions between

- 215 recording methods (i.e. a discrete variable including seven combinations between the recorder 216 type and the trigger sensitivity), using Kruskal-Wallis tests and box plots. We then computed

- 217 the proportion of variance explained by each variable ( _pseudo_ - _R2_ ) to assess whether the 218 importance of the factors of interest (actual drivers of bat activity) was biased by the different 219 recording methods. To properly study the drivers of bat activity at wind turbine nacelles, a

- 220 prerequisite was that the recording methods do not capture an overwhelming part of the

- 221 variance compared to the factors known to affect bat activity. To achieve this, we built one

- 222 full Generalised Linear Mixed Model (GLMM, R package _glmmTMB_ ; Brooks et al., 2017)

- 223 per bat guild, using LRE and MRE activity and SRE occurrence as response variables, and the

- 224 landscape (see Supporting information S2 for landscape variable selection and composition),

- 225 weather conditions (i.e. average wind speed, average temperature and cumulated rain), the

- 226 Julian day, and wind turbine functioning (i.e. average blades rotation speed) and dimensions 227 (i.e. nacelle height and rotor diameter) as fixed effects (hereafter referred to as “explanatory 228 variables”). Since we had a relatively small number of sites, we restricted the number of 229 landscape variables to three; i.e. the same number as the other types of variables (i.e. three

- 230 weather variables and three wind turbine functioning and dimension variables available).

- 231 With such approach, models were always constituted of ten variables, allowing to avoid

- 232 overparameterization. For landscape variables we pre-selected the best computing area buffer

- 233 and in a second step selected the three ones – within the five landscape variables – with the

- 234 best conjoint contributions (see Supporting Information S2 for more details). We used the 235 wind turbine identifier and year as random effects to account for pseudo-replication (i.e. many 236 recording nights per wind turbine) and inter-year variations in activity, associated with a

- 237 negative binomial distribution for LRE and MRE guilds and a binomial distribution for SRE 238 guild (see Supporting information S2 and Table S4 for the composition of full models). Then,

- 239 we computed the _pseudo-R2_ of each variable by subtracting the _marginal R2_ of the full model 240 and that of the model without the target variable, using the R package _sjstats_ .

- 241 The preliminary analysis showed that recording methods resulted in confounding effects with 242 most other variables of interest and captured the largest variance part (Table S5; Figs. 2 & 243 S2). Thus, to model bat activity or occurrence as a function of explanatory variables, we

- 244 selected in a second step only one combination between the recorder type and the trigger

- 245 sensitivity that removed any variation in recording methods. We chose the combination of the

- 246 Batmode set to a trigger sensitivity of 37 dBSPL which had the largest dataset resulting in 34

- 247 wind turbines, 8,619 nights and 65,775 bat passes. Based on this subset, we performed the 248 same GLMMs workflow as presented above (see Supporting information S2 and Table S6 for

- 249 more details) to assess the respective effects of explanatory variables on the LRE and MRE

- 250 activity and SRE occurrence. For each explanatory variable, we checked the potential need for

- 251 adding a non-linear effect by visual inspection of Generalised Additive Mixed Models 252 (GAMM, R package _mgcv_ ; Wood, 2011; see Table 1 for variables that required quadratic or

- 253 cubic effects). We also checked the absence of multicollinearity by calculating the Variance

- 254 Inflation Factor (VIF) for each explanatory variable (R package _performance_ ; Lüdecke et al.,

- 255 2021). All variables showed a VIF<2, implying no evidence of multicollinearity (Chatterjee

- 256 and Hadi, 2006). It should be noted that wind speed and blade speed were not excessively

- 257 correlated thanks to maintenance periods that stopped the turbines in all wind conditions (Fig.

- 258 S3). Overall model validation was performed using diagnostic plots (R packages _DHARMa_

- 259 and _performance_ ;  Lüdecke et al., 2021). Full models were compared to null ones using the

- 260 Akaike information criterion (AIC) (Burnham and Anderson, 2002), and goodness of fit was

- 261 assessed using the marginal _R2_ (variance explained by the fixed effects) and conditional _R2_

- 262 (variance explained by both fixed and random factors) values (Nakagawa and Schielzeth,

- 263 2013). All analyses were performed using a significance threshold of 5% in R statistical 264 software v.4.0.3 (R Core Team, 2020).

- 265

- 266 _2.4. Assessing the effectiveness of using model equations to limit bat exposure compared to_ 267 _conventional curtailments_

- 268 Using the same Batmode dataset, we assessed whether curtailment of wind turbines based on

- 269 multiple-factor models could be more efficient in limiting bat activity exposure at the scale of

- 270 all wind turbines than commonly used blanket curtailment methods. For that, we trained full

- 271 models for each guild on a 50% fully random subset of the dataset (hereafter referred to as

- 272 “training dataset”) and predicted bat activity on the other 50% (hereafter referred to as

- 273 “prediction dataset”), and this 100 times. Then, we computed for each prediction dataset the

- 274 remaining percentage of bat activity (for LRE and MRE guilds) or occurrence (for SRE guild)

- 275 (i.e. the real bat activity or occurrence recorded while the blades were moving) and the

- 276 percentage of lost blade rotations (i.e. as a proxy of lost energy production) resulting of

- 277 curtailing wind turbines following either of two methods: (i) curtailing above thresholds of bat

- 278 activity predicted from full models (hereafter referred to as “multicriteria curtailment 279 algorithm”), and (ii) curtailing below wind speed thresholds and this either without

- 280 temperature threshold or with different minimum temperatures required from 2 to 18°C

- 281 (hereafter referred to as “blanket curtailment”). Finally, we plotted the relationship between

- 282 the remaining percentage of bat activity or occurrence and the percentage of lost blade

- 283 rotations for both curtailment methods to evaluate their effectiveness in limiting exposure

- 284 (Fig. 3A). The comparison of both curtailment methods was conducted for the non-winter 285 periods only.

- 286 To assess whether the effectiveness was relevant for all wind turbines, we also plotted the

- 287 relationship between the remaining percentage of bat activity and the percentage of lost blade

- 288 rotations for each wind turbine independently. We computed Area Under Curve (AUC) values

- 289 for both curtailment methods to evaluate which one was the most effective (i.e. with the

- 290 highest AUC value) (R package _MESS_ ). We also estimated to what extent the effectiveness of 291 curtailment methods was preserved when wind turbines included in the training dataset 292 differed from those in the prediction dataset. For that, we repeated the procedure explained 293 above, but using a training dataset constituted of data from 33 out of 34 wind turbines and a

- 294 prediction dataset constituted of data from the 34[th] wind turbine, and we repeated it for each

- 295 wind turbine to present its results while computing AUC values for both curtailment methods.

- 296 These turbine-by-turbine assessments were only conducted for LRE and MRE guilds for 297 which we had enough data for each wind turbines.

- 298 Finally, because the percentage of lost blade rotations did not constitute a perfect proxy of lost 299 energy production, we assessed whether the relative comparison of lost blade rotations 300 between curtailment methods as a proxy of energy production losses was biased (e.g. one 301 method for a given level of lost blade rotations involving slower blade speeds, and in turn 302 lower energy losses, than the other method). For that we compared the distribution of blade 303 speeds inside lost blade rotations between the two curtailment methods.

## **3. Results**

- 305 _3.1. Bat monitoring_

- 306 A total 98,627 bat passes were recorded at 59 wind turbines and 14,937 nights. However, as

- 307 described above, in order to avoid confounding effects between recording methods and other

- 308 explanatory variables, we only selected wind turbines monitored using Batmode recorders

- 309 which exhibited no trigger sensitivity variation, while including most of the data (i.e. 34 wind

- 310 turbines out of 59 and 8,619 nights out of 14,937). Data from Batmode resulted in a total of

- 311 65,775 bat passes recorded, with 43,519 passes of LRE, 22,135 passes of MRE and 121

- 312 passes of SRE (see Table S3 for species composition). At least one pass of LRE, MRE and

- 313 SRE was recorded in 35%, 18% and 1% of nights, respectively (Table S3).

- 314

- 315 _3.2. Drivers of bat activity around nacelles_

- 316 Full models of bat activity and occurrence showed smaller AIC than null models (delta AIC

- 317 of full models from -50  to -1468), with 33%, 55% and 51% variance explained by fixed

- 318 effects and 78%, 60% and 54% by both fixed and random effects, for LRE, MRE and SRE 319 guilds, respectively (Table S6).

- 320 Regarding landscape variables, LRE activity was positively affected by the landscape

- 321 Shannon diversity index of habitat patches at the 10,000 m radius scale while MRE activity

- 322 increased with increasing patch richness density at the 1,000 m radius scale and forest

- 323 proportion at the 10,000 m radius scale. We also found significant positive relationships

- 324 between SRE occurrence and edge density at the 10,000 m radius scale and the proportion of

- 325 impervious surfaces at the 100 m radius scale (Fig. 4; Table 1). Concerning wind turbine

- 326 functioning and dimensions, increasing average blade speed significantly reduced the

- 327 activity/occurrence of all guilds, while no effect of nacelle height and rotor size were found

- 328 (Figs. 4; Table 1). Concerning weather conditions, average temperature positively and non-

- 329 linearly affected the activity of LRE and MRE guilds, while the average wind speed and the

- 330 cumulated rain negatively affected (non-linearly and linearly, respectively) the 331 activity/occurrence of all guilds (Fig. 4; Table 1). Finally, we found seasonality in the activity 332 of the LRE and MRE guilds, manifested as a cubic and quadratic relationship, respectively,

- 333 with the Julian date: increasing between January and August, and decreasing from September 334 to December (Fig. 4; Table 1).

- 335

- 336 _3.3. Effectiveness of model equations to limit bat exposure compared to conventional_ 337 _curtailments_

- 338 For the blanket curtailment, we found that increasing wind speed thresholds below which 339 wind turbines should be curtailed almost always linearly decreased the real remaining bat 340 activity for all guilds (Fig. S4A-C). For the multicriteria curtailment algorithm, we found that

- 341 decreasing the predicted bat activity above which wind turbines should be curtailed decreased

- 342 the actual bat activity or occurrence exposed: exponentially for LRE activity, logistically for 343 MRE activity and linearly for SRE occurrence. (Fig. S4A-C). Moreover, expanding 344 curtailment increased the percentage of lost blade rotations differently between methods: with

- 345 logistic increases when using wind speed and temperature criteria, and exponential increases

- 346 when using a multicriteria curtailment algorithm. (Fig. 4D-F).

- 347 When we linked the real bat activity or occurrence exposed with the percentage of lost blade

- 348 rotations, we found that the multicriteria curtailment algorithm was more efficient than the

- 349 blanket curtailment for all guilds (Figs. 3B & 5). We found that the multicriteria curtailment

- 350 algorithm at the scale of all wind turbines exhibited on average 20% and 9% less bat activity

- 351 exposed than blanket curtailment without temperature threshold for LRE and MRE guilds,

- 352 respectively, and 24% less occurrence exposed for SRE guild (Fig. 3B1). When blanket

- 353 curtailment included temperature thresholds, the multicriteria curtailment algorithm exhibited

- 354 on average 20 to 29%, 7 to 12% and 24 to 31% less exposure for LRE, MRE and SRE guilds,

- 355 respectively, depending on the temperature threshold considered in blanket curtailment (Figs.

- 356 3B2 & 5). The higher efficiency of the multicriteria curtailment algorithm was confirmed by

- 357 its AUC values which were higher than those of blanket curtailment for a 10°C threshold at

- 358 81 and 75% of wind turbines for LRE and MRE guilds, respectively (Figs. S5 & S6). Finally,

- 359 when the algorithm was trained on 33 out of 34 wind turbines and predictions made on the

- 360 remaining wind turbine(i.e. model training and predictions based on independent sites),

- 361 algorithm curtailment had higher AUC values than blanket curtailment at 81 and 69% of wind

- 362 turbines for LRE and MRE, respectively (Fig. S7 & S8).

- 363 Finally, blade speed distributions did not differ between lost blade rotations of both 364 curtailment methods, thus suggesting that the relative comparison of lost blade rotations

- 365 between curtailment methods as a proxy of energy production losses was not biased (Fig. S9).

## 366 **4. Discussion**

- 367 Identifying drivers of bat exposure to wind turbines from acoustic monitoring at nacelles, and

- 368 the possibility of their combined use as criteria in algorithm-based curtailment, have so far

- 369 received little attention in the scientific literature in the context of wind turbine impact

- 370 mitigation. Our study shows that recording methods should be accounted for when using

- 371 acoustic data continuously produced in post-construction regulatory studies, before analysing

- 372 the drivers of bat exposure. Once detection method biases were avoided, results showed that it

- 373 is possible to disentangle the main drivers. Our findings revealed that landscape features,

- 374 weather conditions, seasonality, and wind turbine functioning determine the activity of all bat

- 375 guilds at nacelles. Algorithms including all these drivers to curtail wind turbines above a

- 376 given level of predicted bat activity are more efficient than common blanket curtailment

- 377 methods based on unique wind speed and temperature thresholds on the activity period of

- 378 bats, as they reduce more exposure while sustaining the same energy production.

- 379

- 380 _4.1. Assessing bias in recording methods_

- 381 One of the aims of this study was to take advantage of the numerous pre-existing data from

- 382 post-construction monitoring studies instead of designing a field study that would require

- 383 paramount monetary and time investments. A prerequisite for using all aggregated data was

- 384 the absence of biases related to the recording methods. Unfortunately, when considering data

- 385 collected using different recording methods, the combination of recorder type and triggering

- 386 sensitivity explained much more variance than all well-known drivers of bat activity (Roemer

- 387 et al., 2019; Behr et al., 2017; Cryan et al., 2014; Horn et al., 2008), minimizing their relative

- 388 importance in the models. All gradients of drivers strongly varied among recorder type/trigger

- 389 sensitivity combinations, thus preventing any modelling of the effects of drivers on bat

- 390 activity based on the full dataset due to confounding effects. Indeed, different recorder

- 391 type/trigger sensitivity combinations can lead to very different levels of bat activity between

- 392 sites due to the different detection distances generated by the material specificities and 393 settings (Darras et al., 2020; Adams et al., 2012). We opted to compensate for this problem by

- 394 modelling the effect of the drivers on bat activity after separating the recorder type/trigger

- 395 sensitivity combinations. However, harmonising monitoring methods across all sites would

- 396 avoid such partitioning and loss of data. Alternatively, future studies could assess the 397 possibility of using corrective coefficients of activity between different recorder type/trigger

- 398 sensitivity combinations, or establish longer bat pass units, to make the sites monitored in 399 different ways comparable.

- 400

- 401 _4.2. Drivers of bat activity around nacelles_

- 402 Our results highlight the high importance of accounting for all drivers (i.e. landscape, wind 403 turbine functioning, weather, and date) to better account for the variation of bat activity at 404 nacelle height. As expected from previous studies looking at fatality risk or bat activity at 405 nacelle height, we found a joint effect of all types of drivers on bat activity (Behr et al., 2017; 406 Thompson et al., 2017; Cryan et al., 2014; Santos et al., 2013; Horn et al., 2008).

- 407 Specifically, LRE and MRE activity increased with the Shannon diversity index of habitat 408 patches and patch richness density, respectively, as previously reported by (Froidevaux et al.,

- 409 2022; Mendes et al., 2017; Monck-Whipp et al., 2017). Edge density also positively affected

- 410 the SRE guild occurrence, as previously documented for hedgerow density (Lacoeuilhe et al.,

- 411 2016; Verboom and Huitema, 1997) or the density of all edge habitats (Ancillotto et al., 2017;

- 412 Mendes et al., 2017). We also found forest cover to positively affect MRE activity, consistent 413 with Roemer et al. (2019), who showed that bat activity at height decreased with the distance

- 414 to the forest, and with Boughey et al. (2011a) who found higher bat activity at ground level 415 with an increasing proportion of forest. Unexpectedly, our model revealed a positive effect of

- 416 impervious habitat proportion on SRE activity, a relationship that is elsewhere described as

- 417 negative (Gili et al., 2020). Impervious habitat in this dataset corresponds to roads and the

- 418 buffer scale selected is very local (100m). This is likely an indirect positive effect related to

- 419 ecotone/hedgerow associated with roads (i.e. road access to a wind turbine), a favourable

- 420 context for foraging of narrow- and edge-space foragers of the SRE guild (Denzinger and 421 Schnitzler, 2013).

- 422 Increasing blade rotation speed logistically reduced LRE activity and SRE occurrence, and

- 423 linearly decreased MRE activity, in accordance with previous studies (Cryan et al., 2014;

- 424 Horn et al., 2008). It should be noted that it is unlikely that this result fully mirrors the effect

- 425 of wind speed because wind speed and blade speed are not fully confounded (Fig. S3). In

- 426 addition, the negative effect of blade rotation speed is preserved at both high and low wind 427 speeds (Fig. S10).

- 428 Regarding weather conditions, increasing temperatures promoted the activity of LRE and 429 MRE guilds, while increasing wind speeds and cumulated rain suppressed the activity of all

- 430 guilds. These results corroborate studies of bat activity at height, showing very similar

- 431 patterns (Wellig et al., 2018; Behr et al., 2017; Horn et al., 2008; Arnett et al., 2006; Redell et

- 432 al., 2006). Interestingly, both LRE and MRE guilds exhibited some tolerance to unfavourable

- 433 weather conditions, with a non-negligible proportion of remaining activity in such conditions

- 434 (see Fig. S11). For instance, above wind speeds of 8m/s, 9% of MRE activity and 12% of

- 435 LRE activity remained; below a temperature of 10°C, 2% of MRE activity and 7% of LRE

- 436 activity remained (Fig. S11), which is highly consistent with findings by Behr et al. (2017) in 437 Germany.

- 438 With respect to seasonality, a peak in LRE and MRE activity was detected in August, thus 439 reinforcing previous studies reporting a peak in bat fatalities at wind turbines in this period 440 (Schuster et al., 2015; Arnett et al., 2008).

## 441

- 442 _4.3. Assessing the effectiveness of using model equations to limit bat exposure compared to_ 443 _conventional curtailments_

- 444 The multifactor responses of bat activity and occurrence at wind turbine nacelles reported in 445 this study highlight the crucial need for curtailment strategies based on all possible 446 combinations of the driving factors, while proving that curtailment based on fixed 447 environmental thresholds such as cut-in wind speed and temperature is not fully effective in 448 avoiding bat exposure.

- 449 Based on the relationship between the percentage of recorded bat activity or occurrence and 450 the percentage of lost blade rotations entailed by each curtailment threshold (i.e. wind speed

- 451 and temperature values for blanket curtailment and a predicted bat activity and occurrence 452 value for multicriteria curtailment algorithm), multicriteria curtailment algorithm will save 453 many more bats from exposure to spinning blades (i.e. on average 20 to 29%, 7 to 12% and 24 454 to 31% less exposure for LRE, MRE and SRE guilds, respectively, depending on temperature 455 threshold considered in blanket curtailment). This result corroborates conclusions from Behr 456 et al. (2017) who performed a similar assessment using the real loss of energy production and 457 curtailment thresholds based on a mean number of fatalities per turbine and per year. The fact 458 that the difference in efficiency is smaller for the MRE than for the LRE guild (both being at 459 high risk of collision; Roemer et al., 2017), is mainly due to the fact that blanket curtailment 460 is significantly less efficient for LREs as they are more tolerant to non-optimal weather 461 conditions (Fig. S11). The increased effectiveness on LRE (the most collision-sensitive guild) 462 reinforces the importance of moving from current blanket curtailments to a multi-criteria 463 algorithm-based approach.

## 465 _4.4. Limitations and recommendations_

- 466 The study calls for prudence when using data from different recording methods that should be

- 467 controlled before any modelling as they could strongly bias the algorithm to use for

- 468 curtailment. This requires regulatory databases (as is the case with the DEPOBIO tool in

- 469 France; https://depot-legal-biodiversite.naturefrance.fr/) to demand the input of metadata

- 470 related to the methods used, or ideally to harmonise these methods. Thus, in order to be 471 generalised to all types of material and settings, the algorithm should either be adapted to each

- 472 type using appropriate data, or a ratio of equivalence in activity between pairs of 473 material/settings should be defined in future studies.

- 474 To go further in the modelling of bat exposure, the curtailment algorithm method we propose 475 should be adapted on an intra-night scale to account for the variation of bat activity during the 476 night and thus minimise even more production losses (Behr et al., 2017). In addition, our 477 efficiency assessment does not rely on a real loss of energy production as such information is

- 478 rarely available from wind energy developers. However, as blade speed distributions do not 479 differ between lost blade rotations of both curtailment methods, the relative comparison of

- 480 lost blade rotations between curtailment methods as a proxy of energy production losses is not 481 biased. Bat activity around nacelles was reported to be a good proxy for fatality risk (Peterson

- 482 et al., 2021; Korner-Nievergelt et al., 2013), but we encourage further research on the

- 483 relationship between activity and mortality to refine algorithms towards an explicit reduction 484 of the real collision risk, either by giving more weight to conditions in which activity is most

- 485 strongly correlated with mortality or by using mortality data directly. Acoustic-informed

- 486 blanket curtailment is another method practised in North America, notably using the Turbine

- 487 Integrated Mortality Reduction (TIMR) system which, in addition to a wind-speed threshold,

- 488 integrates a real-time bat activity criterion. Although this system is not directly comparable to

- 489 our algorithm (intra-night timescale, effectiveness assessed using daily fatality surveys), it

- 490 seems to show similar effectiveness (i.e. a 37% reduction in exposure compared to blanket 491 curtailment) (Rabie et al., 2022; Hayes et al., 2019). Future studies could therefore compare

- 492 these two types of curtailment strategies on an equivalent basis to highlight the strengths and 493 weaknesses of each, especially regarding technological constraints.  Finally, the baseline data

- 494 used to train the algorithm should be updated on a regular basis with data from the latest wind 495 turbine models in order to explicitly incorporate their dimensional changes into the modelling.

- 496 The strategy of algorithm-based curtailment should be conceived on a large scale to save a

- 497 global percentage of the bat community from exposure, although on some sites the method 498 may currently be less effective. In the future, to capitalise on large-scale data, algorithms 499 could be developed using national data and applied site by site as it accounts for the landscape 500 context, and could be regularly updated with data from new post-construction monitoring. 501 This will require more years and sites of monitoring to account for the inter-annual

- 502 stochasticity of the responses and to cover larger landscape gradients, respectively, and would 503 also require updating algorithms with the most recent data to consider climate change and 504 especially the gradual increase in temperature. The large amount of regulatory post-

- 505 implementation acoustic monitoring performed each year could be included annually to

- 506 update algorithms so that the exposure threshold defined by the central authority is 507 continuously based on a predictive tool accounting for climate change. Since temperate

- 508 insectivorous bat species respond to a documented set of landscape characteristics, weather

- 509 conditions and seasonality, we expect the development of such curtailment algorithms to be 510 efficient and of great relevance in most temperate ecosystems.

- 511 Finally, our study calls for the use of multicriteria curtailment algorithms instead of basic

- 512 blanket curtailments as power production is clearly predicted to be higher and the benefit for 513 bats is high in most situations (Behr et al., 2017).
